issue.title: Thames Water's debts: rescue it, or take it back?
issue.question: When a water company can't pay its debts, who should own and run it, and who takes the loss?
issue.summary: Thames Water's holding company has set out a debt rescue plan, with a court hearing on 27 November 2026, creditor meetings on 17 December and a sanction hearing on 13 January 2027. Thames Water Utilities had net debt of £18.5bn at March 2026. The government has ruled nationalising the water sector out of its review of water regulation.
issue.slot_reason: This was the first issue, chosen by hand to try the loop out. A court starts deciding the rescue plan at a hearing on 27 November 2026.

poll.finding: 74% said water companies should be run in the public sector and 6% the private sector. Support for nationalisation falls to 30-31% if it raised bills, borrowing or taxes.

bench.title: Keep Thames Water private, but tie bosses' pay and fines to rivers
bench.answer: Keep the owners and the court rescue. Change the rules attached to it. First, the regulator must ban bonuses and dividends until spills fall for three years running, since part of 2025's fall was dry weather (s5). Second, bosses' pay is held back and can be clawed back if the company breaks the rules. Third, the £122.7m fine is paid in full on its backstop date and not written down (s6). Fourth, a new customer panel gets a seat and a veto on bill rises. Bills do not rise to pay the debts. Ofwat would do this. We would know it worked if spills keep falling in wet years and no bonus is paid.

bench.title: Hand Thames Water to its customers and staff, with debts written down
bench.answer: Put Thames Water into special administration, so a court-appointed administrator runs it while its debts are sorted out (s9 argues this can cost close to zero in law). Then move it into a public-benefit company. Customers and staff elect a board, with seats for river groups. Bosses who broke the rules answer for it, and creditors take the loss before any taxpayer does. Bills do not rise to pay old debts. The government would do this. It worked if spills keep falling in a normal-weather year (s5), the £122.7m fine is paid (s6), and bills stay flat.

bench.title: Let water users own it, and investors take the loss
bench.answer: In this simulation, Parliament would put Thames Water into a trust owned by its water users. Shareholders lose their stake. Lenders take losses instead of passing old debts to bills or taxes. Users and workers elect the board, with local meetings able to demand repairs. Keep staff and water supplies running. Pay managers extra only when independently checked service targets are met. Publish repair spending, spills and board votes. Pursue proven wrongdoing through the courts. Judge success by reliable taps, protected jobs and fewer spills after accounting for rainfall: dry weather helped explain the 2025 fall (s5). Give users the power to vote directors out.

gate.verdict: None of the three passes everything: A and C clear the tests they speak to but leave others open, and B leaves most open. Facts cannot settle who should own Thames Water or who takes the loss.
rejected_claims: B: the court hearing on 27 November is the first step of special administration (s1 describes it as a hearing on the debt rescue plan and does not mention special administration)

jury.question: When a water company fails, who should carry the loss: the owners and lenders, the customers, or the taxpayer?
options: Keep it private and tighten the rules on bosses
Move it to customers and staff, with lenders taking the loss
Let a court-run rescue go ahead, with no change of owner
Take it into public hands, whatever the cost
jury.ruling: Move it to customers and staff, with lenders taking the loss. Five of the twelve jurors wanted the debt to fall on owners and lenders rather than bills or taxes, and a real say for the people who use the water.

reasons.text: Bills have gone up for years while the bosses got paid. Let the people who use the water have the say.
A court should sort the rescue quickly. I don't want a fight over who owns it, and my bills are already high.
Water is too important to leave to shareholders. Put it in public hands and stop the profit-taking.
Keep it running as it is, but make the bosses pay for what they broke. Don't add a new owner to the mess.

minister.trial: In the Thames Water rescue, ask for a customer and staff panel: 12 people drawn by lot from its area, a seat in the creditor talks and a veto on any bill rise that pays old debt. Lenders take the loss first. One company, one panel, no change of owner yet.
minister.fail_number: Any rise in the average Thames Water bill that the company ties to debt payments (target: 0%), or the panel not seated by the 13 January 2027 sanction hearing.
minister.statement: A court hearing on 27 November starts the process on the rescue plan, and the sanction hearing is on 13 January. Thames Water Utilities had £18.5bn of net debt in March 2026. The jury picked a way out. Customers and staff get a say, lenders take the loss. Hard bit: five of twelve jurors is not a landslide, and none of the three answers shows who pays for the pipes. So I'm signing one small thing. One company, one panel of ordinary people with a veto on bills that pay old debts. If bills rise for debt, it failed. If it works, we try a bigger one.

predictions.claim: The court hearing on Thames Water's rescue plan goes ahead on 27 November 2026 without being adjourned.
predictions.rule: True if Thames Water, the court or a major news outlet reports the hearing took place on 27 November 2026. False if it was moved to a later date.

predictions.claim: The court sanctions Thames Water's debt rescue plan by 22 January 2027, after the 13 January sanction hearing.
predictions.rule: True if a court order sanctioning the plan is reported by Thames Water or a major news outlet between 13 and 22 January 2027. False if the court refuses, or has not ruled by 22 January.
